source_text: Res ineptae sunt, et quae stilo nostro convicium magis faciant quam laborem; sed fidem tuam necessario consequuntur. Verumtamen adhuc, ut sit intentus lector, admoneo. Conatus es nempe asserere, quod Dei opus probetur pudendum non esse; sed ut hoc efficere nequivisti, ita spopondisti illud absolutissime, demere te a libidine verecundiam, si opus Dei esse doceatur; quod in primo opere ita approbavi, ut nec te inde putem dubitaturum esse, cum legeris; tamen quoniam hoc commentum tuum significat, necdum ad manus tuas illos venisse libros, id ipsum in praesenti quoque ostendere non pigebit. Irrationabiles igitur animantes, a quo conditas putas, quae certis temporibus ardentissima libidine commoventur, ita ut etiam feritates acuat singularum? Tunc saevus aper, tunc pessima tigris. Ante omnes furor est insignis equarum [n63] . Vere tument herbae. Vere abundantia teneri humoris exuberat. Et coitum certis repetunt armenta diebus [n64] . Longum est ire per singula: omnia genera, quae suspendit volatus, quae demersit natatus, quae sparsit vagatus, per aera, per freta, per nemora, nec tamen aut sublimavit ratio, aut culpa depressit, nota commiscendorum corporum voluptate flammantur. Illum ergo sexuum quem patiuntur ardorem, Dei an diaboli opere susceperunt? Clamabis sine dubio, Dei. Deus ergo sexum naturali voluptate succendit; quod certe consequentius quam tu, Manichaeus negat. Ille enim, a quo concupiscentiam carnis damnare didicisti, quid sibi dicendum esset expendens, rem quam diabolicam definiverat, atque a Dei operibus removerat, quaquaversum eam potuit invenire persequitur; et ideo ut per concupiscentiam corpora hominum, ita per homines, omnes animantes diabolo deputavit auctori. Tu autem, cum in Manichaei castris hactenus manens, maximum eius feras draconem, de quo infelicibus mentibus per naturale malum et crimina nuptiarum lethale inspiras venenum; non vis tamen in omnes naturas suggesta a magistro tela iaculari; et brutis familiarior (quibus tamen ob hoc parcis, ut rationabilium statum auctoratius crimineris), consentis in illorum corporibus Deum fecisse, quod in nostris diabolum; cum tamen id ipsum, sed mitius in hominibus, quam in pecoribus esse fateare. Ut ergo quid sit effectum, prudens lector accipiat, libidinem corporum in animalibus factam a Deo non negas. Non est ergo Dei operibus indigna illa affectio, quae in his substantiis acrior invenitur, quae nihil de diaboli malo, vel tenui voluntate rapuerunt. Ergo quia concupiscentia defensa est exemplo animalium, defensa etiam dignitate auctoris sui, nec mala, nec diabolica est, quam fecit Deus formator corporum, et quam tenet ea quae est expers natura peccati; cum hoc ergo claruit, inquiro utrum istam libidinem, quam corpora humana persentiunt, Deum fecisse consentias? Si annueris, sublata contentio est, tu emendatus, et Manichaeus permanebit attritus. Si autem dixeris: In corporibus hominum a Deo non potuit fieri; refero, illam voluptatem et concupiscentiam carnis, hominis te, non Dei operibus indignam putare. Ambigi quippe non potest, quoniam si quod confiteris a Deo ubicumque factum, hoc dicas in homines fieri nequivisse, non concupiscentiae testimonia aufers debita, sed humano corpori conquiris indebita. Vide ergo cuius profanitatis sit sectae tuae finis. Dicis esse indignum carne mortalis, quod indignum non fuit opere Conditoris. Igitur hoc sensu non libidinem vituperasti; sed hominem, quem accusare volueras, extulisti. Talem habet constantiam talemque mercedem, qui veritati indicit bellum, ut contrariis semper conatui suo feriatur effectibus. Ego ergo nunc tuis verbis consequentius, sicut omnis prudentia cognoscit, insurgo. Itane in taxandis et exprimendis operibus Dei, non auditur ratio, non omnium naturarum considerantur exempla [n65] ; sed in tantum hominis effertur insania, ut putet inconveniens suis esse visceribus, quod per Dei operam in naturae suae cernit vigere consortibus? Neque enim alia nostrorum corporum est, vel origo, vel ratio, quam mutuorum.
pass_a_gloss: The things are foolish, and such as make insult rather than labor for our pen; but they necessarily follow your faith. Nevertheless I still advise that the reader be intent. You have tried indeed to assert that a work of God is proved not to be shameful; but as you were unable to accomplish this, so you promised most absolutely that you would take reverence away from lust if it should be taught to be a work of God; which in the first work I so approved that I think you will not even doubt it when you have read; nevertheless because this invention of yours signifies that those books have not yet come to your hands, it will not be irksome to show the same thing also in the present. The irrational living beings, therefore, by whom do you think them founded, which at certain times are moved by most burning lust, so that it even sharpens the ferocities of each? Then the savage boar, then the worst tigress. Before all the fury of mares is outstanding. In spring the grasses swell. In spring the abundance of tender moisture overflows. And the herds repeat coupling on certain days. It is long to go through each: all kinds, which flight has hung, which swimming has sunk, which wandering has scattered, through air, through straits, through groves, and yet neither has reason raised them nor fault pressed them down, are inflamed by the known pleasure of mingling bodies. That ardor of the sexes therefore which they suffer, did they receive it by the work of God or of the devil? You will cry without doubt, of God. God therefore kindled sex with natural pleasure; which certainly Manichaeus denies more consequently than you. For he, from whom you learned to condemn the desire of the flesh, weighing what must be said for himself, pursues the thing which he had defined as diabolical and had removed from God's works wherever he could find it; and therefore as through desire the bodies of humans, so through humans he assigned all living beings to the devil as author. You however, remaining thus far in Manichaeus's camps, bear his greatest dragon, from which you breathe lethal poison into unhappy minds through natural evil and the charges of marriages; you do not want nevertheless to hurl at all natures the weapons suggested by the master; and more familiar to the brutes (whom nevertheless you spare for this, that you may more authoritatively accuse the status of rational beings), you consent that in their bodies God made what in ours the devil made; when nevertheless you confess that the same thing is milder in humans than in cattle. Therefore, that a prudent reader may receive what has been effected, you do not deny that the lust of bodies in animals was made by God. That affection is therefore not unworthy of God's works, which is found sharper in those substances which have snatched nothing of the devil's evil even by a thin will. Therefore because desire has been defended by the example of animals, defended also by the dignity of its author, it is neither evil nor diabolical, which God the former of bodies made, and which that nature holds which is without share of sin; when this therefore has become clear, I inquire whether you consent that God made that lust which human bodies feel? If you shall have granted, the contention is removed, you are amended, and Manichaeus will remain worn down. But if you shall have said: In the bodies of humans it could not be made by God; I reply that you think that pleasure and desire of the flesh unworthy of the works of the human, not of God. For it cannot be doubted that if what you confess was made by God anywhere, you say could not be made in humans, you do not take away testimonies owed to desire, but you seek for the human body things not owed. See therefore of what profanity the end of your sect is. You say it is unworthy of mortal flesh, what was not unworthy of the Founder's work. Therefore by this sense you have not blamed lust; but you have lifted up the human whom you had wanted to accuse. Such constancy and such a wage he has who declares war on truth, that he is always struck by effects contrary to his attempt. I therefore now rise more consequently by your words, as all prudence knows. Is it so that in assessing and expressing the works of God, reason is not heard, the examples of all natures are not considered; but the insanity of the human is so lifted up that he thinks inconvenient for his own viscera what he sees thriving through God's work in the partners of his own nature? For neither is the origin or the reason of our bodies other than of those of the mute.

pass_b_english: These are foolish matters, which insult my pen more than they burden it. Yet they follow necessarily from your belief. Still, I again urge the reader to pay attention. You tried to assert that whatever is proved to be God’s work is not shameful. Though you could not establish that, you committed yourself most clearly to this: you would remove shame from lust if it were shown to be God’s work. I proved this so thoroughly in my first work that I do not think even you will doubt it once you read it. Nevertheless, since this invention of yours indicates that those books have not yet reached your hands, I will not shrink from demonstrating the same point here as well.

Who, then, do you think created the irrational animals? At certain seasons they are stirred by the most ardent lust, so that it even sharpens each species’ ferocity: “Then the boar is savage, then the tigress most cruel”; “Above all, the frenzy of mares is remarkable” (Virgil, Georgics 3.248, 266). In spring the grasses swell; in spring an abundance of tender moisture overflows; “And the herds seek mating on their appointed days” (compare Virgil, Georgics 2.324–331). It would take too long to go through them one by one. Every kind of creature—held aloft by flight, submerged by swimming, or scattered by wandering through air, sea, or woods, yet neither raised by reason nor lowered by guilt—is inflamed by the familiar pleasure of bodily union. Did they receive the sexual ardor they experience through God’s work or the devil’s? You will undoubtedly cry out: God’s. So God kindles sex with natural pleasure. Manichaeus, to be sure, denies this more consistently than you do.

For the man from whom you learned to condemn the desire of the flesh considered what he must say. He pursues wherever he can find it the thing he had defined as devilish and removed from God’s works. Thus, through desire he assigned human bodies to the devil as their author, and through human beings he assigned all living creatures to him. But you still remain in Manichaeus’s camp and carry his largest dragon standard, from which you breathe deadly poison into unhappy minds by teaching natural evil and the criminality of marriage. Yet you refuse to hurl the weapons your teacher supplied against all natures. Friendlier to the beasts—though you spare them only to accuse the condition of rational creatures with greater authority—you agree that God made in their bodies what the devil made in ours, although you admit that the same thing exists in human beings more mildly than in animals.

Let the thoughtful reader understand what has been established. You do not deny that God made bodily lust in animals. This feeling is therefore not unworthy of God’s works, since it is found more strongly in substances that have taken nothing of the devil’s evil, not even by the slightest act of will. Desire, then, is defended by the example of animals and by the dignity of its author. What God, the maker of bodies, made, and what a nature free of sin possesses, is neither evil nor devilish. Once this is clear, I ask whether you agree that God made the lust experienced by human bodies. If you agree, the dispute is over: you will be corrected and Manichaeus will remain crushed. But if you say, “It could not have been made by God in human bodies,” I reply that you consider this pleasure and desire of the flesh unworthy of human works, not God’s. There can be no doubt: if you acknowledge something was made by God somewhere, yet say it could not have been made in human beings, you are not taking away the testimony due to desire but seeking an undeserved distinction for the human body.

See, then, how profane your sect’s conclusion is. You call unworthy of mortal flesh what was not unworthy of the Creator’s work. By this reasoning you have not disparaged lust; you have exalted the human being you meant to accuse. Such is the consistency, and such the reward, of someone who declares war on truth: he is always struck by results opposite to his efforts. I will therefore now rise against you with a more consistent use of your own words, as every sensible person recognizes. Can it be that when God’s works are assessed and described, reason receives no hearing and the examples of all natures receive no consideration (compare Augustine, On Marriage and Concupiscence 2.9.22)? Does human madness rise so high that a man thinks unsuitable for his own flesh what he sees flourishing through God’s work in creatures that share his nature? For the origin and constitution of our bodies are no different from those of these creatures.

Julian's pudenda libido is the appetite accompanying union, not a created substance of sin.
